title: Ganesh Chaturthi: welcoming Ganesha home
hook: clay Ganeshas are carried home with drums, kept for days, then given back to the water
carry: welcome it, then let it go
tomorrow: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess

segments.voice: Yesterday: Janmashtami from the kitchen, a cradle at midnight and a tower for a pot of yogurt. Your line was the good arrives at midnight. Did you prepare something for someone? Day six hundred seventy-eight.

Here's a strange rule some families keep on Ganesh Chaturthi. With a clay Ganesha just carried home, drums still echoing in the street, a grandmother says: whatever you do tonight, don't look at the moon. Kids who've never heard it before immediately want to look. Why would anyone be told not to look at the moon on Ganesha's own birthday? Because, people say, Ganesha and the moon once had a very bad evening.
screen: `A CLAY GUEST, JUST ARRIVED.` → `DON'T LOOK AT THE MOON TONIGHT.` → `A VERY BAD EVENING.`

segments.voice: The story, as it's told, goes like this. On his birthday, Ganesha has been offered modak after modak, the sweet dumplings, and he's eaten them all. Late at night, very full, he's riding home on his mouse. A snake crosses the path. The mouse panics, Ganesha tumbles off, and his belly splits, modaks rolling everywhere. In some tellings he ties his belly back up with the snake. And up in the sky, the moon, proud of his beauty, laughs at him. Ganesha, embarrassed and furious, curses the moon: whoever looks at you will be falsely accused. The moon is horrified. The gods come to plead. And here's the part worth noticing. Ganesha softens. He doesn't take the curse back completely, but he narrows it: it will hold only on this one night, the fourth day of his month. That's why some families keep their eyes down on Chaturthi night. Tradition even names someone it happened to. In some tellings, Krishna glimpses the moon on Chaturthi and is soon accused of stealing a famous jewel, the Syamantaka. The Bhagavata Purana tells the jewel story, how Krishna was suspected and had to go and find the jewel to clear his name; the link to the moon comes from other tellings. People say that hearing the jewel story lifts the curse if you looked by accident. Underneath the comedy is a small teaching about anger. Ganesha's embarrassment was real. He didn't pretend it wasn't. But he let most of it go.
screen: `TOO MANY MODAKS, ONE SNAKE.` · `THE MOON LAUGHS.` · `A CURSE, THEN SOFTENED.` · `KRISHNA AND THE SYAMANTAKA JEWEL.` · then, large: `HE LET MOST OF IT GO.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Recall a recent moment when someone laughed at you, or you felt foolish. Let yourself feel it again, just a little: the heat in the face, the urge to snap back. Hold it, the way you'd hold something heavy in both hands. Then, on a slow out-breath, set it down. Not all of it, maybe. Just most of it. Rest with what's left. The bell holds the time.
Ganesh Chaturthi. Ganesha's fourth day, and the night, people say, not to look at the moon, after the god who softened his own curse.
Your line: welcome it, then let it go. Today, when something embarrasses you, feel it fully for a moment, then let most of it go. Day six hundred seventy-eight.

screen: `DAY 678 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NAVARATRI: NINE NIGHTS OF THE GODDESS.`

howItsDone: Some Hindu families avoid looking at the moon on the night of Ganesh Chaturthi, and some read or hear the Syamantaka jewel story as a remedy if they see it by accident.

fork.setup: you're Ganesha. the moon laughed at your fall and you cursed it. now the gods are pleading for the moon. what do you do?
options: keep the curse as it is.
soften it to one night a year.
fork.reveal: in the telling, Ganesha narrows the curse to Chaturthi night. not all forgiven, but most of it let go.

original.note: Sanskrit and Marathi modaka: a sweet dumpling, often of rice flour with coconut and jaggery, Ganesha's favorite.

trapdoor: what you thought: not looking at the moon is a superstition with no story.
what it means: it comes from a story of Ganesha's anger, softened.
what a scholar hears: the Syamantaka episode is in the Bhagavata's tenth book; its link to seeing the moon on Chaturthi comes from other Puranic and popular tellings.
